issues.description: The problem statement and the template define the addParent method as addParent(Person person, Person parent) (person first, parent second). In the solution implementation the method declaration swaps the parameter names (public Person addParent(Person parent, Person person)), which is semantically inconsistent with the described parameter order and the intended meaning of the parameters. This naming swap in the solution's implementation can confuse students reading the solution or comparing behavior, and it risks producing incorrect behavior because the implementation uses the parameters assuming the template/spec ordering.
issues.suggestedFix: Rename the parameters in the solution's addParent method to match the specification/template: change the signature to public Person addParent(Person person, Person parent) and update the method body to treat the first parameter as the child (person) and the second as the parent. This alignment preserves the intended semantics and avoids student confusion when comparing template, problem description, and solution.

issues.description: The conceptual method addParent(Person person, Person parent) is described in the problem statement and declared in the template with the parameter order/names (person, parent), but the solution implementation declares the same method with parameter names reversed (parent, person). Although parameter names do not affect compilation, this naming reversal breaks the direct mapping between the problem description/tests (which treat the first argument as the child/person and the second as the parent) and the solution code, creating unnecessary cognitive load for students trying to relate requirements, tests, and implementation.
issues.suggestedFix: Rename the parameters in the solution's addParent method to match the problem/template: change method signature to addParent(Person person, Person parent) and update internal references accordingly so the first parameter clearly represents the child/person and the second the parent. This aligns implementation, tests, and the exercise description and reduces cognitive friction.
